unit: Following a severe bout of typhoid, Adrian was advised by his doctor to seek recovery near the ocean. He traveled to the coastal area of Seven Gulls to view the old homestead of his grandparents, the Tremaynes. During his summer stay, he spent mornings writing and afternoons engaging in outdoor excursions, fishing, and boating with the Carrow family, Lorna Vane, and Captain Saul. During this time, he collaborated with James Garrick to write The Life-Book of Captain Saul, taking a photograph of Captain Saul that was later included in the volume. He fell deeply in love with Lorna Vane, though he wrestled in private over his feelings. After returning from his summer stay, he received word that his manuscript was accepted for publication. Later, while residing in Vancouver, he wrote to arrange another month's room and board, returning to court Lorna.

passages.v04:c22:p0019: “I am going to visit Lorna to inquire whether she would accept a paying guest,” Miss Winifred continued. “Yesterday, a letter reached me from a Mrs. Daly living in Toronto, who stayed as a boarder with me briefly two years past. She requested that I accommodate a friend of hers during the summer. Adrian Treleaven is his name, and he works as a journalist, and it appears he is the grandson of the schoolmaster by whom this house was erected. The eldest daughter of John Tremayne was wedded to an Ontario resident called Treleaven, and he is her child. He wishes to view the ancient homestead where his grandparents resided. A severe attack of typhoid afflicted him during the spring from which he has not fully recovered, so he was instructed by his physician to go to the ocean. Going to the hotel does not appeal to him—a peaceful domestic environment is all he desires. Taking him in is impossible for me, because I must be absent throughout August. My appointment as a delegate to the W.F.M.S. conference in Portmaris has occurred and I am attending it. Whether Lorna will care to take the trouble of accommodating him is also unknown to me, but no other option exists. Should she be unable to accept him, he will be obliged to go across the harbor.”
passages.v04:c25:p0014: Adrian Treleaven engaged in writing during the morning hours. The afternoon period was usually occupied by a cheerful excursion alongside the Carrows. Lorna frequently joined them as well, because Captain Saul regularly assumed responsibility for Rufus so that she could be liberated. During the evening hours they wandered through the low-lying, daisied, coastal pastures beneath a golden moon, or else they gathered inside the living room of the small house where the chill of the ocean wind frequently made a driftwood fire welcome, discussing the endless topics that joyful, enthusiastic, intelligent youth are capable of discovering to converse about.

value: Barney Pullen vastly admired Nell Harcourt.
unit: Barney Pullen drove a double-seated buggy alongside his sister Odette to transport Nell Harcourt and Isolde to an event in Pale Sands, feeling immense pride in traveling beside Nell, whom he vastly admired. During a gathering with the local youth, he occupied a corner all night, observing Nell with a joyful smile. Having been given the upper farm by his father, Barney sought to marry Nell, but his extreme bashfulness led him to incessantly persuade Odette to propose on his behalf. After Nell firmly rejected the proposal, Barney quickly turned his attention to Nettie Scobie, whom he subsequently married, entering the Gorham Pullen pew with his new bride glowing with satisfaction and joy.

Out from town, a group of visitors was anticipated, and following the concert, the performers were to be served a supper.
passages.v03:c02:p0004: Every member of the “old crowd” had gathered, packed with glee, enthusiasm, and young vivacity. There was Isolde Pembroke, flush-cheeked and marked with dimples, closely followed by the loyal Gideon; Odette Pullen, tidy, practical, and unadorned; Opal Pettigrew, appearing at her most attractive and radiant wearing a cream silk blouse, her blonde hair adorned with red geraniums; Hugh Carrow alongside Wilfred Mott, each attempting to remain as close to the slippery Nell as they could; Carrie Mott, appearing washed-out and somber due to rumors that her father had forbidden Oliver Kimball from approaching the location; Elias Purdy MacKinnon, possessing a circular face and repulsive ears that remained precisely as circular and repulsive as always; and Barney Pullen, who occupied a corner for the entire night, let out quiet laughs whenever somebody addressed him, and observed Nell Harcourt with a joyful smile across his wide, freckle-covered face.
passages.v03:c08:p0012: “Yours, naturally,” Odette replied. “Barney desires to make you his wife. He has perpetually been mad about you—and currently father has bestowed the upper farm upon him under his own name, so there is no obstacle to stop him from taking a bride. However, he is so bashful that he was unable to inquire directly whether you would take him, which led him to persuade me to act on his behalf. I would have preferred not to, but he harassed me incessantly until I promised that I would, provided a suitable opportunity arose. What is your opinion on the matter, Nell?”
passages.v03:c08:p0015: “It probably didn't,” concurred Odette. “Courting is something Barney has constantly been much too timid to consider. Even so, you could reflect upon it, Nell. He lacks any negative vices, works extremely hard, and is someone you can count on. ‘A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.’ He instructed me to inform you that he would be entirely agreeable to waiting until your college education is finished, should you demand it, even if his preference is a wedding this spring prior to the start of planting. I believe that as soon as Barney is certain you refuse to have him, he will choose Nettie. Please do not speak of this to anybody, will you, Nell?”

unit: Tabitha Pratt lived as an unwed woman from the Glen. She was hired as a general servant at the small residence of Dr. Carrow and his wife Nell. After visiting a sick person in the Glen, she returned to her duties and grew deeply devoted to Nell, affectionately referring to her as "young Mrs. Doctor." Though initially suspicious of Thirza Abernethy's arrival, she accepted her once she saw Thirza did not interfere with her kitchen duties or her care of Nell. She took pride in her cooking, competing in mind with Miss Tolley, and assisted Nell in hosting social gatherings. She also endured the presence of the First Mate, a pet cat, despite having little affection for felines.

passages.v04:c18:p0052: Without deigning to answer, Miss Winifred addressed Tabitha Pratt instead, a stern-visaged, good-natured aged unwed woman from the Glen, who had been employed for a few weeks as a general servant at the small residence. Having gone to the Glen to visit an ill person, Tabitha had only recently come back.
passages.v04:c19:p0000: At the start of June, during a time when the sand hills displayed a grand splendor of pink wild roses and apple blossoms enveloped the Glen, Thirza came to the little house along with a black horsehair trunk decorated with brass nails, a chest that had rested untouched in the Grey Shutters garret for fifty years. Tabitha Pratt had spent her few weeks' stay at the little house growing to adore “young Mrs. Doctor,” her name for Nell, with an unreasoning devotion, causing her to view Thirza with a somewhat envious suspicion initially. However, because Thirza refrained from meddling with affairs in the kitchen and displayed no wish to hinder Tabitha's care of young Mrs. Doctor, the loyal servant made peace with her being there, informing her friends in the Glen that Miss Abernethy was a splendid old woman who understood her place.
passages.v04:c19:p0041: “Indeed, I am aware of that, as I have experienced the same feeling regarding different matters. Nevertheless, every one of us holds you dear, Nell.
